entries.title: Broadview 6 hearing set to rock Chicago federal courthouse, but DOJ official could intervene
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/11/02/fbi-boutros-depodesta-broadview-six" target="_blank" >stage is set</a> for a historic showdown inside Chicago’s federal courthouse, where a judge has ordered the city’s top federal prosecutor<b> </b>to testify — and made clear she<b> </b>doesn’t believe what he’s told her<b> </b>about the disastrous “Broadview Six” scandal.</p><p>U.S. Attorney <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/04/07/chicago-crime-justice-department-doj-boutros-trump-midway-blitz-corruption" target="_blank" >Andrew<b> </b>Boutros</a><b> </b>is<b> </b>due<b> </b>on the witness stand<b> </b>later this month. So are three prosecutors from his office. Sanctions<b> </b>and criminal contempt charges loom. And finger-pointing has already begun over the failed 2025<b> </b>prosecution<b> </b>of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/06/01/broadview-six-midway-blitz-abughazaleh-straw-rabbit-perry-trump-ice-crime" target="_blank" >six Midway Blitz protesters</a>.</p><p>U.S. District Judge <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/17/broadview-six-judge-april-perry-trump-vance" target="_blank" >April<b> </b>Perry’s</a><b> </b>hearing<b> </b>could take the Dirksen Federal Courthouse deep into uncharted waters — if it goes down. That remains to be seen, thanks in large part to a new character in the case: Associate<b> </b>Attorney<b> </b>General<b> </b>Stanley Woodward.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/11/02/fbi-boutros-depodesta-broadview-six" >‘Broadview 6' case heats up again as ex-FBI boss sues, top federal prosecutor ordered to testify</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Woodward is the Justice Department’s third-highest ranking official. He’s increasingly at the center of Justice Department controversies, and he appears to have taken the wheel in the Broadview Six litigation. He publicly <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/30/controversial-doj-boss-takes-reins-in-tainted-broadview-6-case-stymies-judges-inquiry" target="_blank" >inserted himself</a> into the case Oct. 30.</p><p>Woodward is expected to challenge Perry and try to short-circuit her hearing, which she’s said will take place by<b> </b>Nov. 24. No such challenge has surfaced yet, though, and<b> </b>the<b> </b>Justice Department has<b> </b>declined<b> </b>to comment.</p><p>The day Woodward entered the Broadview Six case, Woodward<b> </b>also faced off with U.S. District<b> </b>Judge<b> </b>Ana<b> </b>Reyes<b> </b>in Washington. The pair tangled over a golf course President Donald Trump has sought to renovate in the nation’s capital,<b> </b>in an exchange that seemed to solidify Woodward’s defiant reputation.</p><p>The exasperated Reyes<b> </b>told Woodward<b> </b>early on, “let’s not play games anymore,”<b> </b>according to a transcript of the hearing.</p><p>That did little to bring the temperature down.</p><div At one point, the judge<b> </b>accused Woodward of trying to take back an argument he’d made.</p><p>“Here’s the thing,” she<b> </b>told Woodward, “you just said it. There’s literally a transcript of it. Now, if you want to correct yourself and say ‘gosh, that’s not what I meant,’ by all means.”</p><p>“Gosh, that’s not what I meant,” Woodward replied.</p><p>Later, the judge asked<b> </b>Woodward<b> </b>about the golf course itself. She<b> </b>told him, “you’re the one who’s a golfer, not me.”</p><p>“I have golfed,”<b> </b>Woodward replied. “I would not describe myself as a golfer.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/17/broadview-six-judge-april-perry-trump-vance" >‘Broadview 6' judge has to decide whether to hold prosecutors accountable after exposing misconduct</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Particularly frustrating to the judge, it seemed, was Woodward’s refusal to interpret Truth Social messages<b> </b>from<b> </b>Trump.</p><p>“We’re not on TV,” Woodward<b> </b>told her.<b> </b>“I mean, I’m not a pundit opining about the president’s words.</p><p>“As you’ve reminded me multiple times, I’m the No. 3 ranking official at the Department of Justice.”</p><p>And now, Woodward’s at the center of the “Broadview Six” case.</p><h3><b>What does Judge Perry want to know?</b></h3><p>Perry made her purpose clear during a hearing Oct. 1: “My sole focus, at this point, is on lack of candor, concealment of material facts, or other misconduct that occurred before me.”</p><p>In other words, she wants to know whether she was lied to during the Broadview Six prosecution.</p><p>The case revolved around a protest outside an immigration holding facility in west suburban Broadview in September 2025. Prosecutors alleged that a crowd pushed and damaged a federal agent’s SUV.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/27/broadview-six-boutros-chicago" >What to know about the ‘Broadview Six’ scandal rocking Chicago’s federal courthouse</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>But from that crowd, only six people were charged with a conspiracy to impede the agent. Most of them were involved in local Democratic politics, raising questions about selective prosecution.</p><p>The case collapsed after Perry discovered apparent misconduct by Boutros’ staff while they sought an indictment against the group from a grand jury. Assistant U.S. Attorney Sheri<b> </b>Mecklenburg<b> </b>allegedly spoke to grand jurors outside the grand jury room, for example.</p><p>While the initial controversy revolved around <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/22/broadview-six-damage-spreads-boutros-drops-more-charges-details-ongoing-review" target="_blank" >Mecklenburg’s alleged misconduct</a>, Perry has since turned her attention to the accuracy of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/09/feds-appear-to-hide-name-of-government-lawyer-in-new-broadview-six-court-filing" target="_blank" >two<b> </b>claims</a><b> </b>made by the feds<b> </b>last spring.</p><p>The first revolved around whether the White House played any role in the case. Boutros’ team told Perry<b> </b>in March<b> </b>there were “no communications of any nature from, to, or with anyone outside [the U.S. attorney’s office] (other than the local FBI investigators assigned to the case) regarding any investigatory or charging decisions.</p><p>“To be crystal clear, this specifically includes anyone in the White House” or at Justice Department headquarters in Washington, prosecutors wrote.</p><p>That claim <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/11/02/broadview-six-depodesta-boutros-kat-abughazaleh" target="_blank" >has been undermined</a> by a recent lawsuit brought<b> </b>against<b> </b>Boutros<b> </b>by<b> </b>former<b> </b>Chicago<b> </b>FBI<b> </b>boss<b> </b>Douglas<b> </b>DePodesta.</p><div class="Enhancement" Attorney General Todd Blanche, FBI Director Kash Patel and Assistant Attorney General Colin McDonald. Blanche is now the attorney general.</p><p>“During this meeting, Defendant Boutros discussed the Broadview Six investigation with his superiors in the Department of Justice and other law enforcement officers,” DePodesta’s attorneys wrote in the lawsuit.</p><p>That meeting would have happened two days before<b> </b>Boutros’ office<b> </b>first<b> </b>tried<b> </b>to<b> </b>secure<b> </b>an<b> </b>indictment<b> </b>against the Broadview Six.</p><p>The judge has also zeroed in on Boutros’ claim that<b> </b>he<b> </b>learned of alleged<b> </b>wrongdoing<b> </b>by Mecklenburg in late April. He’s<b> </b>since<b> </b>acknowledged<b> </b>receiving<b> </b>a<b> </b>transcript<b> </b>in<b> </b>October<b> </b>2025<b> </b>that<b> </b>documented some of her alleged misconduct.</p><p>Boutros<b> </b>said<b> </b>he<b> </b>didn’t remember<b> </b>reading it.</p><p>But grand jurors<b> </b>initially<b> </b>rejected the Broadview Six case. The feds went back to the panel twice, records show. And<b> </b>Perry<b> </b>pointed out that “Boutros himself had to approve the re-presentment of the case to the grand jury.”</p><p>“The idea that [U.S. Attorney] Boutros would have made such a significant decision without reviewing the best evidence available to him about what went wrong in the grand jury is nearly unfathomable,” Perry wrote.</p><h3><b>Who is Stanley Woodward?</b></h3><p>Woodward entered the Broadview Six case fresh off his showdown with Judge<b> </b>Reyes<b> </b>in<b> </b>Washington. But he’s been at the center of other recent Justice Department controversies.<b> </b></p><p>In May, Woodward<b> </b>signed<b> </b>the settlement agreement<b> </b>between<b> </b>the president and the IRS that<b> </b>established<b> </b>the controversial “anti-weaponization fund”<b> </b>for people claiming to be harmed by “lawfare”<b> </b>and the weaponization of the justice system.</p><p>He signed that deal<b> </b>three days before<b> </b>the Broadview Six case collapsed. Members of the group <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-house/2026/05/28/broadview-6-trump-blanche-doj-justice-department-weaponization-fund" target="_blank" >actually once mused</a> about applying to the fund — but<b> </b>Blanche<b> </b>later<b> </b>issued an order insisting<b> </b>the<b> </b>fund<b> </b>was<b> </b>rescinded<b> </b>“beyond any doubt.”</p><p>Woodward’s name also appears<b> </b>at the top of the Justice Department’s Oct. 22<b> </b>lawsuit<b> </b>over an entry<b> </b>into<b> </b>the<b> </b>Alaska<b> </b>Senate<b> </b>race<b> </b>by a candidate<b> </b>with a similar name to Sen. Dan<b> </b>Sullivan. That lawsuit has<b> </b>already<b> </b>been<b> </b>tossed<b> </b>by a judge,<b> </b>though the Justice Department<b> </b>has filed an appeal.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div He<b> </b>alleged<b> </b>one<b> </b>made<b> </b>“unethical”<b> </b>comments<b> </b>to The New York Times about the Trump administration’s deportation efforts.</p><p>“The American people will undoubtedly question” whether the judge can be impartial, Woodward<b> </b>wrote.</p><p>Finally, upon entering Chicago’s Broadview Six case, Woodward<b> </b>told<b> </b>Judge Perry<b> </b>she<b> </b>should<b> </b>clarify<b> </b>whether<b> </b>a<b> </b>previous<b> </b>“request”<b> </b>she’d<b> </b>made<b> </b>for<b> </b>records<b> </b>was really meant to be a “directive.”</p><p>But<b> </b>“for the avoidance of doubt,”<b> </b>he wrote, “the United States has not agreed to provide any information.”</p><p>And, he<b> </b>made clear, “the United States believes further proceedings would not be appropriate.”</p><h3><b>What will happen at the hearing?</b></h3><p>There’s no obvious playbook for Perry’s hearing. entries.title: 8-year-old Alex Anning brings 500 bags of groceries to Englewood families
entries.summary: <p>Alex Anning was 7 years old when his family had to drive past a homeless person begging for money because the traffic light had turned green. Anning couldn’t shake the memory out of his head and decided he wanted to make a difference.</p><p>For his 8th birthday last year, he led his first grocery drive, with the support of his mother, Kymbria Young-Anning, executive director of Season to Soar, a nonprofit focused on helping the next generation become leaders who serve their communities.</p><p>“I’m so honored that an epitome, an example of a leader with a servant heart and global perspective, is my own son Alex,” Young-Anning said.</p><p>Alex, who turns 9 Monday, organized another grocery giveaway Friday afternoon at the Montessori School of Englewood. Throughout the event, which saw dozens of residents and parents line up to pick up groceries, Alex never slowed down, darting between volunteers and chatting up attendees while handing out multiple grocery bags at a time.</p><p>In partnership with the Illinois Network of Charter Schools, organizers prepared 500 grocery bags stocked with items including bread, pasta sauce, macaroni and cheese, meat, milk and vegetable oil.</p><p>Kikanza Harris Scott, director of community impact at the Illinois Network of Charter Schools, said the event was particularly important as community members continue to face food insecurity, including those who have lost access to Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits. Organizers raised more than $5,000 for the event, Scott said.</p><p>“If kids don’t have the food and the essentials that they need, it’s hard to do anything else,” Scott said.</p><p>Many people turned out to volunteer at the event, including a group of graduate students from the University of Chicago Divinity School. They helped pack the grocery bags, carry them to tables in an outdoor area near the playground and distribute them to parents and residents who stopped by.</p><p>Annika Fuller, 24, volunteered as part of the service project committee at Disciples Divinity House at the University of Chicago. Fuller said practicing servant leadership is central to her denomination, Disciples of Christ.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure Hermitage Ave. The giveaway, organized in celebration of Anning’s birthday, provides 500 bags of free groceries to families in the community</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“And so by doing a project like this, it’s really living out what I believe to be my calling,” Fuller said. “My calling is to help people, not just throw money at the problem, but actually like boots on the ground, interacting with people, talking to them face to face, making sure they feel loved and understood and cared for.”</p><p>After all the bags were set outside, Young-Anning spoke to the volunteers and kids, sharing that the event was also to honor the recent death of Javits Frimpong, a 15-year-old student from Ghana who was shot and killed in New York City last week. Anning said the death hit close to home because her husband is Ghanaian. </p><p>“When things like that happen, we respond by just continuing support into the community and lifting up positive values in youth, which is why we decided to honor Javits ... to send a message to young people that instead of being violent and bullying one another, to be kind and giving,” Young-Anning said.</p><p>Abenaa Adjei, 30, whose 8-year-old son attends the school, learned about the event on Facebook and stopped by while picking him up. Alex said, before volunteers set out to distribute groceries and the parents started lining up.</p>

entries.title: Longtime Rogers Park ties deepen grief of family killed in townhome fire
entries.summary: <p>It was 6 a.m. Thursday when sisters Angelita Sanchez and Vanessa Garcia learned through a news report the Rogers Park townhome where their sister, mother and two nephews lived was on fire. </p><p>They later received the devastating news <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/11/05/4-killed-in-rogers-park-fire" target="_blank" >that their relatives had died</a>. </p><p>The victims were identified by relatives as Valentino Vallejo, 13; Francisco Vallejo, 24; Mariza Garcia, 48; and Maria Jimenez de Garcia, 69.</p><p>For Sanchez, the tragedy is also the loss of a family matriarch who held her daughters together, particularly after their father died during the COVID-19 pandemic.</p><p>“We’re women power. She was the head of the woman power,” Sanchez said of her mother. “We’re family bound.”</p><p>A day later, as relatives searched their charred home at 7049 N. Paulina St. for belongings and keepsakes, neighbors and strangers stopped to offer condolences, prayers and donations.</p><p>Among them was Ellen Baren, who lives a couple of blocks away. Although she didn't know the family, the news of the fire and the deaths hit her deeply. She walked to the home to pay her respects, but began to cry as she approached.</p><p>“It's sad because all of a sudden it started and all of a sudden, you know, it was over. Their lives were over,” Baren said.</p><p>Standing across the street, Baren sang a Jewish prayer: “May your memory be for a blessing.”</p><p>“The prayer isn't so much about someone passing away as much as it is to live a good life,” Baren said.</p><p>As the sisters kept watch over their family home, they confronted not only the loss of four loved ones but the difficult prospect of arranging four funerals.</p><p>“Four bodies, four burials,” Vanessa Garcia said. “That's hard. Times are hard already, and for us to think about the amount of money that's gonna cost. It's sad to say, but you do worry about that.</p><p>A<a class="Link" href="https://www.gofundme.com/f/help-our-family-lay-our-loved-ones-to-rest?attribution_id=sl%3Aff8ab178-97a3-4601-9499-90426015ac41&ts=1793925026&utm_campaign=fp_sharesheet&utm_content=amp30-control&utm_medium=customer&utm_source=sms" target="_blank" > GoFundMe</a> campaign launched Thursday had raised about $87,000 by Friday evening to assist with costs toward a $140,000 goal.</p><p>The cause of the fire remains under investigation. Family members said the home had working smoke detectors. Chicago Fire Department personnel were also at the scene Friday distributing smoke detectors and fire safety information to residents, <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/CFDMedia/status/2118743595763040418?s=20" target="_blank" >according to a department post on X.</a></p><p>Mayor Brandon Johnson, who visited Rogers Park Friday as part of his Working People Neighborhood Tour, called the deaths an “absolute tragedy.”</p><p>“Lives in communities are not the same when tragedy like that occurs, and so we are praying for the families and all entries.title: Chicago parking attendants reach deal with operators to end strike
entries.summary: <p>Chicago area parking attendants have reached an agreement with the Chicago Parking Association after launching what was characterized as an unfair labor practice strike, the Teamsters Local 727 union announced Friday.</p><p>The strike began four days ago after the union's nearly 1,200 members voted down the Chicago Parking Association's "last, best, and final" offer, deeming it "disrespectful," the union said in a statement.</p><p>The union was bargaining with the company over its contract that expired last week, when 98% of voting members authorized a strike, alleging the parking association was negotiating in bad faith.</p><p>On Tuesday, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/11/03/parking-attendant-strike-teamsters-ohare-mccormick-hyatt" target="_blank" >members began picketing at O’Hare Airport</a>, McCormick Place and the Hyatt Regency. </p><p>By Friday afternoon, more than 30 separate unfair labor practice charges were pending. A Sunday night Chicago Bears game at Solider Field was fast approaching, with no workers to provide parking.</p><p>That was when the agreement was reached, which the union's Secretary-Treasure John Coli, Jr. said was a "major victory."</p><p>"The terms of this new agreement protects bargaining unit work against emerging technologies, increases PTO, provides a new retiree benefit and will provide the largest benefit and wage increases ever achieved by the Union in the parking industry," he said in the statement. </p><p>On Tuesday, parking operations continued normally at O’Hare and at McCormick Place despite the picket, both sites confirmed. </p><p>Representatives for Hyatt Regency did not respond to a request for comment.</p><p>Parking operations are expected to resume immediately, a Chicago Parking Association spokesperson said in a statement on Friday.</p><p>“The Chicago Parking Association is pleased to have reached a settlement with Teamsters Local 727," the spokesperson said. "We look forward to continuing to serve our customers throughout Chicagoland... We appreciate our customers’ patience throughout this process and are excited to move forward together.”<br></p>

entries.title: Bears QB Caleb Williams refining his potential by embracing simplicity, delivering efficiency
entries.summary: <p>Caleb Williams isn’t ready to admit he has settled down.</p><p>He’s gotten smarter and sharper, embracing some of the simple fundamentals of playing quarterback, and vaulted himself into the MVP race and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a> into Super Bowl contention. He is, as the Bears hammered to him in the offseason, getting more while doing less.</p><p>It was evident in the season opener and even more so in the last three games since returning from a hamstring injury. There’s less running wild, more precision from the pocket. Fewer highlights, but far more efficiency.</p><p>He’s embracing that boring can be beautiful.</p><p>“I had a couple pretty cool scrambles,” he argued. “I still do all of that.”</p><p>One play he probably was thinking of as he interjected was early in the third quarter <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/02/bears-big-plan-coming-together-beautifully-as-34-17-win-over-seahawks-pushes-them-to-best-start-since-2012" >against the Seahawks</a>, when he dropped back, slipped on the turf and ended up in the arms of defensive tackle Leonard Williams.</p><p>But instead of racking up mileage running sideline-to-sideline as he looked for an opening, Williams rolled a few steps to his right and — just as blitzing safety Nick Emmanwori closed in on him from behind — fired a dart over the middle to Rome Odunze for 22 yards.</p><p>“I’ve just grown in certain aspects,” Williams said. “I’ve tried to maintain the things that I’ve done well, and then the things that I haven’t done well, just try and up those.”</p><p>Confirmed: They’ve been upped.</p><p>When the Buccaneers see him for the first time Sunday night at Soldier Field, they’ll wish they’d gotten a shot before he learned all this. He’s always had high-end talent, but now he’s built pillars underneath it: self-control in the pocket, more accurate passing, quicker reads, better anticipation of defensive coverages.</p><p>Williams has been unstoppable over his last three games. In wins over the Falcons, Patriots and Seahawks, he completed 73.8% of his passes, averaged 286.7 yards, thrown four touchdown passes with no interceptions and posted a 111.3 passer rating.</p><p>As exciting as he was at times last season, he never did that. Not even close, really.</p><p>The quarterback who was last in the NFL in completion percentage last season at 58.1 is now second at 70.9. That led to a jump from 6.9 to eight yards per pass. He went from 69.8% of his passes being on target last season, according to Pro Football Reference, to 78.9%, and that bumped the Bears from 10th in yards after catch to fifth.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/08/31/why-do-so-many-people-hate-bears-qb-caleb-williams-he-answers-exactly-that-question" >Williams</a> has been as nonchalant about his progress as he was when he discussed attacking those weaknesses in the offseason. When asked after the Seahawks game about seeing that work materialize as more efficiency on the field, he asked, “Uh, how efficient was I?”</p><p>A 101.0 passer rating and 70.6 completion percentage.</p><p>“Cool, cool,” he replied.</p><p>He continued, “The work that you put in, when it shows up and you can find ways to be consistent, it’s another motivating factor for me that I’m doing something right. I need to keep going. I need to keep finding ways to get better.”</p><p>Continuing to fine-tune the basics is essential to that.</p><p>Williams contradicted himself slightly when he reflected on seeing the value in base hits passes rather than always swinging for the fences.</p><p>All he did was fire deep in high school, and at USC he remembered “very little” interest in taking checkdowns. He spent his rookie season running for his life in a terrible offense with a shaky offensive line. He started to see the light last season under coach <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/16/bears-coach-ben-johnson-is-not-here-merely-to-win-we-want-to-be-feared" >Ben Johnson</a>, who had helped the Lions’ Jared Goff become one of the NFL’s most surgical quarterbacks, and now their mindsets have further merged.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/11/as-engineer-and-artist-blend-styles-bears-ben-johnson-gets-goosebumps-about-future-with-caleb-williams" >When Johnson talked to the Sun-Times in training camp about the project</a> of blending Williams’ artistry with the machinelike approach that this playbook is built for, he was clear he didn’t want to turn Williams into Goff, but added, “That doesn’t mean that he can’t share more of those attributes.”</p><p>The silver lining of his strained hamstring is that indirectly reinforced some of what Johnson had been teaching.</p><p>Williams was already on the right path — the difference was undeniable in the opener against the Panthers — but while he was out, he watched 38-year-old third-stringer Case Keenum carve up the Eagles by simply putting the ball in the right place at the right time.</p><p>And while Williams would almost certainly reject this, it’s logical that his mobility would be limited as he plays through the injury, and that might make him more inclined to stay in the pocket as well. He rushed for a combined 64 yards in the last three games, one fewer than he had in the season opener alone.</p><p>Williams hasn’t lost himself in his development. Hamstring injury or not, he’s still ready to improvise with mesmerizing scrambles and rare cross-body passes if the need arises. When it’s break-glass-in-case-of-emergency time, no one does it better.</p><p>But he’s not relying on that anymore. That’s what it looks like when a talented young quarterback starts refining his potential and delivering production.</p>

entries.title: Vecinos devastados luego de que cuatro miembros de una familia mueren en incendio en Rogers Park
entries.summary: <p>Un incendio arrasó una casa del vecindario de Rogers Park la madrugada del jueves, matando a una familia de cuatro, incluyendo un niño de 13 años y su perro, dijeron la policía, testigos y una concejal.</p><p>El niño de 13 años fue identificado como Valentino Vallejo, estudiante de octavo grado de la primaria Kilmer International Academy, en un correo electrónico enviado a las familias escolares por la directora Natalie Rodríguez.</p><p>Rodríguez dijo que la escuela dispondrá de consejería para el duelo y otros apoyos para los estudiantes, y que dará información sobre los funerales cuando esté disponible.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-060000" name="module-060000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>"Estamos devastados por la noticia de un trágico incendio en una vivienda de nuestra comunidad esta mañana y por la pérdida de uno de nuestros alumnos de octavo grado del CPS y de miembros de su familia", decía el comunicado. "Nuestros pensamientos están, ante todo, con los familiares de este estudiante, sus seres queridos y la comunidad escolar".</p><p>Dos mujeres, de 69 y 46 años, y un hombre de 22, fueron hallados sin responder en la casa de dos pisos alrededor de las 4:15 a.m., dijo la Policía de Chicago.</p><p>Fueron trasladados a hospitales del área, donde fueron declarados muertos, señaló la policía.</p><p>Sus nombres no se dieron a conocer de inmediato, según la Oficina del Médico Forense del Condado de Cook.</p><p>Angelita Sánchez organizó una <a class="Link" href="https://www.gofundme.com/f/help-our-family-lay-our-loved-ones-to-rest" target="_blank" >página de GoFundMe</a> para ayudar con los gastos funerarios. Las víctimas eran su madre, su hermana y dos sobrinos.</p><p>"Simplemente no hay palabras para describir el dolor de perder no a uno, sino a cuatro seres queridos a quienes amamos profundamente, todos al mismo tiempo", se lee en la descripción de la colecta. "Nuestros corazones están destrozados, y estamos enfrentando una realidad para la que nunca pudimos habernos preparado".</p><p>Elise Adu, que vive dos pisos abajo del lugar donde inició el incendio en 7049 N. Paulina St., se despertó al escuchar a sus vecinos gritar desde su ventana pidiendo ayuda. Uno de los miembros de la familia, dijo, gritó que "no tenían su teléfono".</p><p>Recordó haber pensado, "esto no puede ser real".</p><p>"Agarré mi teléfono y corrí al cuarto de mis padres y dije, 'Algo está pasando afuera, tenemos que llamar al 911'", dijo Adu, de 27 años.</p><p>Después de que ella, sus padres y su perro salieran, fue a despertar a los vecinos. Y un pensamiento terrible se apoderó de ella.</p><p>"Seguí pensando que si alguien estaba adentro, no iba a sobrevivir", dijo.</p><p>Adu veía a la familia —una abuela, la madre y dos nietos— todos los días. A menudo les dejaba sus llaves cuando salía de viaje con su familia.</p><p>"Es una tragedia horrorosa perder a una familia entera", dijo la concejal Maria Hadden (49.°), al Chicago Sun-Times. "Tenían un perro que paseaban, y mucha gente los conocía. Eran una familia encantadora. Duele mucho".</p><p>Hadden confirmó que la página de GoFundMe, que había recaudado más de $84,000 el viernes y seguía subiendo, fue organizada por la familia de las víctimas.</p><p>Hadden confirmó que el perro, que Adu dijo era un Labradoodle marrón de 4 años llamado Remi, murió en el incendio.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item"> <bsp-carousel entries.title: Iowa recruit Jake Thies breaks Robert Spillane's Fenwick career TD record
entries.summary: <p>The son of Fenwick's athletic director, Jake Thies grew up on the Friars' football sidelines.</p><p>One of the players he looked up to was Robert Spillane, a running back and linebacker in high school. Undrafted out of Western Michigan, Spillane is now an established NFL veteran in his ninth pro season and his second year as a starting linebacker for the Patriots.</p><p>Last week, Spillane's Fenwick record for career touchdowns fell. The new record holder, with 41 TDs? Thies.</p><p>The Iowa commit scored three touchdowns in three different ways — a run, a reception and a pick-six — in a 38-20 Class 6A second-round win against Highland Park.</p><p>He'll try to add to the record Saturday afternoon when Fenwick (7-3) goes to Hononegah (9-1) in the 6A second round. Thies was quick to share the credit after a practice this week.</p><p>"[The record] definitely means a lot." he told the Sun-Times. "The four years of high school, I've been putting in a lot of work, taking coaching, and [I] really just couldn't do it without my coaches, my teammates. Everyone believes in me, and my coaches have always been really hard on me because they know the potential I have."</p><p>What Thies didn't say about the record, Fenwick coach Matt Battaglia did.</p><p>"I don't think people even realize that Jake had a thumb injury his sophomore year so he wound up playing only defense because he had a club on," Battaglia said.</p><p>What people did realize last year is that Thies is one of the state's elite two-way players.</p><p>The 6-foot, 185-pounder made plenty of big plays on both sides of the ball, especially in Fenwick's 38-28 upset of East St. Louis in the 6A title game. Thies ran nine times for 100 yards — including scores of four and 74 yards — caught three passes for 61 yards and ran an interception back 43 yards.</p><p>What to do for an encore?</p><p>"He's put in the work in the offseason," Battaglia said. "He developed his body. He never missed a workout. So I think you see a lot of that with how powerful a lot of his runs have been, [and] his tackles. That's just more development in the weight room, getting a year older — just natural development to go with his talent."</p><p>Thies also had the chance to learn from Spillane, who comes back to Fenwick in the summer.</p><p>"I feel like the biggest thing that I've taken from him is how hard you need to play," Thies said. "You've got to be the hardest worker, the hardest player on the team."</p><p>Last year, Thies had his older brother Tommy by his side. Now Tommy is a freshman defensive back at Miami (Ohio) and Jake has taken over some of his leadership responsibilities. Battaglia said Tommy was the vocal one and Jake "was more the introverted one.<br>"And this year, especially on defense, you see him take over as that quarterback of the defense and making the checks, making the calls, getting guys aligned right."</p><p>Battaglia, one of the state's top young coaches with two state titles in his first six seasons, said he's often asked where Thies ranks among the players he's had/</p><p>"It's like children," Battaglia said. "You can't commit to any one. But the one thing we can commit to and say without a doubt with Jake is his football IQ on both sides of the ball are as good as — he's probably smarter than some coaches out there. Ir's elite level football knowledge that he has. ...</p><p>"He understands the big picture."</p>

entries.title: New Trier keeps the party rolling, beats Homewood-Flossmoor to advance to the 8A quarters
entries.summary: <p>There’s a unique energy on the New Trier football sideline this season. The Trevians are having fun. That’s probably what high school football should be about, but for many high-level programs—especially this late in the playoffs—every moment feels like it carries life-or-death stakes, and the pressure can be tremendous.</p><p>“That is not what it is like here,” Trevians linebacker Declan O’Meara said. “If you make a mistake, someone has your back, and if you make a good play, everyone goes crazy. We are confident and prepared, and we trust each other. When you aren’t worried about letting people down and don’t have that pressure, it makes football a very fun sport.”</p><p>There’s been a lot of winning with that fun this season. And it continued on Friday, as the Trevians knocked off Homewood-Flossmoor 26-23 in the second round of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/10/17/ihsa-state-football-playoff-pairings-class8a-illinois-2026" >Class 8A</a> playoffs. This is the first time New Trier has advanced to the state quarterfinals since 2014.</p><p>“It is just this group,” New Trier coach Brian Doll said. “They have kind of enjoyed it from freshman year on. The seniors are really tight and great leaders. They are having a lot of fun. We all are now. We have had a real culture change the last two years, led by those guys. We came to work every day this week, and we were having a blast.”</p><p>Purdue recruit Jackie Ryder, a 6-5 senior, is the special talent who has elevated the Trevians’ program. He was 13 of 31 passing for 130 yards and two touchdowns.</p><p>New Trier’s final drive took five minutes off the clock to secure the win.</p><p>“We knew we had the talent, but not many people thought this,” Ryder said. “It is only the sixth time the school has gone to the quarterfinals. It is an awesome feeling. I am so happy I get to keep playing football with these guys. It is the most special group of individuals I’ve been around.”</p><p>Ryder also had seven carries for 54 yards. Most of the runs were key plays that kept drives alive.</p><p>“[Ryder] ran a lot more than usual,” Doll said. “I’ve been pretty protective of him. But tonight he had to run the ball, and he took some big shots. He did a good job, and I’m proud of him.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-f40000" entries.title: Luke Hernandez's big night showcases Oswego's depth in a second-round win against Naperville North
entries.summary: <p>Luke Hernandez isn't the first or second option for Oswego's run game, but you couldn't tell that on Friday night.</p><p>The senior fullback rumbled for a pair of 49-yard runs that helped the Panthers hold off Naperville North 21-19 in a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/10/17/ihsa-state-football-playoff-pairings-class8a-illinois-2026" >Class 8A</a> second-round game.</p><p>Oswego (10-1) plays the winner of Saturday's game between Lyons and Bolingbrook next week in the quarterfinals.</p><p>Hernandez's first long run got the Panthers out of a hole on their own four-yard line. That second-quarter drive ended with a TD run by Drew Kleinhans.</p><p>"We were like, all right, we're kind of pinned back really far and we've just got to pound it," Hernandez said. "Then it just broke through. Great block by Graham Schwab, [he] just pummeled some kid, and I just broke free."</p><p>Did he think he might go all the way?</p><p>"No, I kind of ran out of go-go juice," Hernandez said with a smile.</p><p>But he didn't on his second and last carry of the game. That went for a touchdown on the third play from scrimmage in the third quarter, pushing Oswego's lead to 21-0</p><p>"I was just running and I thought I was going to get ankle-bit around the 20-yard line, so I kind of got close to [the Naperville North] defender," Hernandez said. "I thought I was going to get taken down [but] I just dragged him with me."</p><p>All in all, it was a much bigger statistical night than usual for the Kankakee Community College baseball commit.</p><p>"I'm usually just focused on blocking," Hernandez said. "I'll get a nice little fullback dive here and there."</p><p>His blocks are usually for junior Ammar Banire, who had 24 carries for 120 yards on Friday in his second game back after being sidelined by injury for more than a month.</p><p>"It was very hard in the beginning," Banire said of his layoff. "But then I started to adapt. I started to learn new stuff, teach the other guys something — just continue to make us better as a team."</p><p>Still, there's no question the Panthers — who were second in 8A last year — are at their best when Banire is on the field.</p><p>"He's a lot of everything," Oswego coach Brian Cooney said. "It's the talent, it's the emotion ... if he's on the field, you know where he's at. So it sets up other guys for success."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-070000" entries.title: Illinois becomes bowl-eligible with home win over Nebraska
entries.summary: <p>CHAMPAIGN — Collin Dixon caught two touchdown passes including a record-breaker and Illinois used a trick play to set up its go-ahead TD as the Illini defeated Nebraska 24-13 on Friday night to become bowl eligible with their fourth straight victory.</p><p>Dixon’s 3- and 6-yard TD receptions gave him 12 for the year, breaking Illinois’ all-time single-season by two. He caught eight passes for 129 yards from Katin Houser, who was 22 of 36 through the air for 292 yards and three TDs.</p><p>A 29-yard run by holder Lars Rau on a fake field goal set up the go-ahead TD for Illinois (6-3, 4-2 Big Ten Conference) early in the third quarter — a 5-yard pass from Houser to Jordan Anderson. Rau is the Illini's punter.</p><p>Nebraska (5-4, 2-4) lost its fourth straight. Anthony Colandrea was 32 of 43 for 284 yards and a TD to Jacory Brown Jr., who had six catches for 93 yards. Jamal Rule ran for 69 yards on 15 carries.</p><p>Dixon scrambled into the end zone on a 3-yard TD pass from Houser late in the first half on his record-breaking reception to tie the game 7-7 at halftime.</p><p>Nebraska took a 7-0 lead early in the second quarter on a 15-yard run by Mekhi Nelson on his only carry of the game. The Huskers drove 98 yards in 10 plays for the score.</p><p>Nebraska kicker John Hohl missed 54- and 45-yard field goals in the half.</p><p><b>The Takeaway</b></p><p>Nebraska: The Huskers got off to a 5-0 start this season for the first time since 2016, then suffered three straight heartbreaking losses by a total of 13 points. They led each of those games in the fourth quarter, irritating their rabid fanbase. Nebraska’s loss Friday night won’t help matters in Lincoln.</p><p>Illinois: Early-season home losses to Duke and Purdue seemingly put a damper on the Illini’s bowl chances. But Illinois has bounced back with four straight wins, much needed victories heading into a tough stretch to end the regular season (at No. 5 UCLA, home vs. No. 21 Iowa and at Northwestern). Only UCLA (5-0) has a longer Big Ten winning streak than Illinois, which is eligible for a third straight bowl appearance for the first time since 1992.</p><p><b>Up next</b></p><p>Nebraska: At Rutgers on Nov. 14.</p><p>Illinois: At No. 5 UCLA on Nov. 13.</p>
